The investigation also included farms in New Mexico where cattle were experiencing similar symptoms such as decreased lactation and low appetite. Officials believe wild migratory birds introduced the virus, as deceased wild birds were found on the properties. Federal agencies assured the public there was no concern for the safety of the commercial milk supply, as milk from sick cows is diverted or destroyed and pasteurization inactivates the virus. The news, however, did impact the market, with cattle futures falling due to uncertainty and fears of reduced consumer demand. Prediction target period: from 2025-02-28 to 2025-03-19. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> During the CattleFax Outlook Seminar at CattleCon 2025 in San Antonio, Texas, meteorologist Matt Makens of Makens Weather LLC forecasted that a La Niña weather pattern would introduce volatile weather changes across North America in the winter of 2025. The forecast indicated that drought conditions are expected to intensify across the Western U.S. during the spring and expand into the Pacific Northwest, the Northern Plains, and the Canadian Prairies through the summer. These weather developments are anticipated to be a critical factor influencing the availability of grazing and feed for cattle. <2> Analysts predict that beef and cattle prices, which reached record levels in 2024, will average new highs throughout 2025. [6] The primary drivers for this forecast are a multi-year tightening of cattle supplies and persistently strong consumer demand. [1] The U.S. cattle inventory began 2025 at its lowest level since 1951, marking the sixth straight year of contraction. [3] While a slow herd expansion may begin, significant rebuilding is not anticipated until 2026 or later, constrained by factors like dry weather, high interest rates, and labor shortages. [1, 3, 9] This tight supply is expected to cause U.S. beef production to decline. [6] Concurrently, beef demand in the United States is the strongest it has been in 40 years. [1, 9] Specific forecasts project fed steer prices to average $201 per hundredweight (cwt), a notable increase from 2024. [3] As a result of lower domestic production, beef exports are projected to fall while imports are expected to rise. [3, 5] <3> Based on a U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) report released on January 31, 2025, the U.S. cattle inventory continued to contract as of January 1, 2025, marking the smallest herd since 1951. The USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) confirmed that the total number of cattle and calves was 86.7 million head, down about 1% from the previous year. Economists noted that this continued tightening of supply would almost certainly lead to higher beef prices for consumers later in 2025. <4> A historic winter storm, described as a "once in a generation" event, struck the Southern United States in late January 2025. [3] The event was initiated by an Arctic blast that moved into the region on Sunday, January 19, bringing record-breaking low temperatures and fueling the storm. [5] Between January 20 and 22, the storm delivered unprecedented snowfall to parts of Texas and Louisiana. [4, 5] On January 21, the Beaumont-Port Arthur area in Texas recorded 4.5 inches of snow, its snowiest day since records began in 1901. [5] That same day in Louisiana, Baton Rouge received a record 7.6 inches (the most since 1892), and New Orleans saw a record 8.0 inches (the most since 1948). [5] The extreme cold and snow created significant challenges, with ranchers in East Texas and the Mississippi Valley working to protect their cattle. [3, 9] The National Weather Service in Lake Charles, LA, issued its first-ever blizzard warnings for parts of the state. [5] <5> Cattle and beef markets started 2025 strong, reaching new record price levels in the first half of January without the typical post-holiday dip. [1] For the week ending January 17, 2025, the 5-market fed steer live price was $203.56 per hundredweight (cwt), a 17.3% increase from the previous year. [1, 3] In Oklahoma auctions during the same week, the price for 500-pound steers (M/L, #1) rose to $361.88/cwt, which is an 18.1% increase year over year. [1, 3] <6> An analysis of the restaurant industry in 2024 reveals a challenging year for many operators, with several key factors impacting performance. Concerns over slowing consumer demand, overall market volatility, and persistent inflation negatively affected restaurant stocks throughout the first half of the year and beyond. The median restaurant stock concluded 2024 with a 4.8% decrease, and a majority of publicly traded restaurant companies saw their stock values end the year in negative territory. A notable trend was the slowdown in foot-traffic growth, particularly impacting fast-food chains which experienced weak traffic. While some input costs, like beef, showed signs of stabilization and potential decline, this was not enough to offset the broader economic pressures. In October, same-store traffic growth was still negative at -2.5% year-over-year, though this marked an improvement from the previous month. Despite these difficulties, overall restaurant sales were projected to rise in 2024, though higher operating costs continued to squeeze profit margins. <7> A year-end market review confirmed that cattle and calf prices continued an upward trend in the fourth quarter of 2024. In the Southern Plains, prices for 500-600 pound steers increased by approximately $40 per hundredweight (CWT) between early October and mid-December. The review, published on December 31, 2024, noted that fed steer prices in the same region reached $195 per CWT as of mid-December 2024. <8> In early October 2024, analysts noted that despite seasonal tendencies for calf prices to decrease, limited cattle numbers were expected to drive feeder prices higher. This assessment proved accurate, as prices for 500-600 pound steers in the Southern Plains increased by approximately $40 per CWT from early October to mid-December, a trend attributed to a reduced number of calves. These market conditions unfolded amidst significant drought in the central and southern plains, affecting large portions of Texas, Oklahoma, and Tennessee. The drought created an incentive for the earlier-than-usual marketing of calves and feeder cattle, which analysts suggested could spread out the typical fall price low over a longer period. <9> On November 22, 2024, Mexico's Chief Veterinary Officer officially notified the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) of a New World screwworm detection. [3, 5, 6, 7] The pest was discovered in a cow in the southern Mexican state of Chiapas, near an inspection checkpoint by the Guatemalan border. [3, 5, 6, 7, 8] New World screwworm larvae infest the living tissue of warm-blooded animals, including livestock and humans, which can lead to severe infections and potentially death if untreated. [3, 4, 6, 7, 10] In response to the significant threat posed to U.S. agriculture, APHIS immediately suspended the importation of ruminants, such as live cattle and bison, that originate from or transit through Mexico. [8, 10] This action was taken to prevent the pest from entering the country while authorities gather more information on the extent of the infestation. [4, 6]

[2, 3, 4, 7] An additional non-tariff barrier impacting trade was China's failure to renew establishment registrations for the majority of U.S. beef plants and cold storage facilities, which had expired in March. [2, 6, 11] While the critical Chinese market saw a sharp decline, the overall impact on U.S. beef exports was partially offset by growth in other markets, including South Korea, Japan, and Central and South America. [2, 4, 6] <2> A report from Catalina's Shopper Intelligence Platform released on April 16, 2025, indicated that grocery price inflation for the 'Meats, Poultry and Eggs' category saw an 8% year-over-year increase in the first quarter of 2025. The notable increase in the meats, poultry, and eggs category was offset by a decrease in the prices of fruits and vegetables and a modest 1% increase in the cost of cereal and bakery products. <3> A report from early April 2025 highlighted the significant impact of multi-year droughts on U.S. beef prices. [14] Persistent dry conditions, particularly in states like South Dakota, severely diminished pasture grass for the upcoming 2025 grazing season. [2, 14] Much of South Dakota, for instance, had received 50% or less of its normal precipitation since October 2024. [6] This lack of forage forced ranchers to either purchase more expensive feed or reduce their herd sizes by sending cattle to slaughter prematurely. This downturn, attributed to a financially 'stretched' consumer base, resulted in sales declines for many major QSR chains. Among the segments, only Casual Dining and Fast Casual managed to achieve positive same-store sales growth. Specific performance issues were reported by major brands, including a 3.6% drop in U.S. comparable sales for McDonald's, a 2.8% decrease in U.S. same-restaurant sales for Wendy's, and comparable sales declines of 1% for KFC and 5% for Pizza Hut. <5> In its "Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Outlook" report for March 2025, the USDA increased its 2025 beef production forecast by 120 million pounds to a total of 26.685 billion pounds. [1, 3] The report was published on March 17, 2025. [1, 3, 9] This tight supply is expected to cause U.S. beef production to decline. [6] Concurrently, beef demand in the United States is the strongest it has been in 40 years. [1, 9] Specific forecasts project fed steer prices to average $201 per hundredweight (cwt), a notable increase from 2024. [3] As a result of lower domestic production, beef exports are projected to fall while imports are expected to rise. This reduction in cattle supply contributed to record-high prices for slaughtered steers during the first quarter of 2025. The USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) confirmed that the total number of cattle and calves was 86.7 million head, down about 1% from the previous year. Economists noted that this continued tightening of supply would almost certainly lead to higher beef prices for consumers later in 2025. <9> A historic winter storm, described as a "once in a generation" event, struck the Southern United States in late January 2025. [3] The event was initiated by an Arctic blast that moved into the region on Sunday, January 19, bringing record-breaking low temperatures and fueling the storm. [5] Between January 20 and 22, the storm delivered unprecedented snowfall to parts of Texas and Louisiana. [4, 5] On January 21, the Beaumont-Port Arthur area in Texas recorded 4.5 inches of snow, its snowiest day since records began in 1901. [5] That same day in Louisiana, Baton Rouge received a record 7.6 inches (the most since 1892), and New Orleans saw a record 8.0 inches (the most since 1948). [5] The extreme cold and snow created significant challenges, with ranchers in East Texas and the Mississippi Valley working to protect their cattle. [3, 9] The National Weather Service in Lake Charles, LA, issued its first-ever blizzard warnings for parts of the state. [5] <10> Cattle and beef markets started 2025 strong, reaching new record price levels in the first half of January without the typical post-holiday dip. [1] For the week ending January 17, 2025, the 5-market fed steer live price was $203.56 per hundredweight (cwt), a 17.3% increase from the previous year. [1, 3] In Oklahoma auctions during the same week, the price for 500-pound steers (M/L, #1) rose to $361.88/cwt, which is an 18.1% increase year over year. [1, 3]
